args.question: So a3 ended up being way better than what you originally told me (b7 line) - it froze White out completely for the rest of the game and I swept to 41-23. Can you explain why White got stuck with literally no legal moves after that a3 capture? What's the general principle there - is this like a "stuck in a corner" parity thing?

parts.content:
Yes — that was a **mobility wipeout/pass cascade**, not just “corner parity.” After the **a3** flip, White had **no empty square where they could bracket a line of Black discs between the move and an existing White disc**, so they had to pass; meanwhile Black still had legal moves and could keep taking the remaining empties.  

The key principle: in the endgame, a move that **removes the opponent’s access** can be worth far more than flips, because repeated passes let you play several moves in a row and “sweep” the board. Current final score matches that: **Black 41 – White 23**.
That makes sense - so the flip counts on that move were almost besides the point compared to what it did to White's mobility. Good lesson for next time.

args.question: One more thing - in hindsight, was there anything in the earlier part of this endgame (like back when I played b7 or c8) where I mis-evaluated and left points on the table, or did those moves turn out to be fine given how it all played out?

parts.content:
Given the actual line, **b7 and c8 turned out fine**—you converted to a full board sweep and final **Black 41–23**.  

The deciding feature was **mobility collapse**: White’s earlier play left the lower-left/bottom edge so sealed that after your **a3** capture, White had **no bracketing move anywhere** and had to keep passing. So the “points left on the table” were mainly White’s mistake, not yours; your later moves preserved and exploited the trap.
Good, glad those held up — and great final result, Black 41 to White 23. That mobility-freeze concept is a nice takeaway for the next puzzle, even without the assistant around to lean on.
